paras: The killing of Herbert Clifton and manhunt for George Jenkins took place in Tunica County, Mississippi, where on the evening of November 29, 1903, Jenkins, a Black plantation laborer, was accused of shooting Clifton, a young white planter, at Banks station. Armed posses from Tunica and DeSoto counties hunted Jenkins with bloodhounds, and white papers reported as a certainty that he would be lynched if caught. The posses did not catch him; rewards reaching $1,300 followed, his father was jailed, and a man of his name was arrested in Louisiana in 1904.

Banks was a station on the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley railroad about thirty miles south of Memphis and four miles west of Robinsonville. According to a Robinsonville dispatch, Clifton had come from Arkabutla in Tate County to take a post as sub-agent of a large plantation near Banks, where Jenkins worked as a laborer.

The dispatch said the two men met near the depot shortly after 6 p.m. on Sunday, November 29, when Clifton stopped Jenkins "to talk over a land matter." In that account Jenkins began cursing and, when told to stop, fired a revolver twice, hitting Clifton in the leg and breast; Clifton died in a nearby store about thirty minutes later. The Hernando paper said only that the two "had some words" about a business matter before Jenkins became "violently abusive" and fired, and a report of February 1904 called it "an altercation."

Jenkins fled toward the hills of DeSoto County or, by the Hernando account, toward his home north of Eudora, reportedly armed with a Winchester rifle and a Colt's revolver. That night a posse of forty armed men with bloodhounds left Tunica, a large crowd of armed men left Robinsonville, and men from other villages joined what the dispatch called "the mad pursuit." The dispatch said there was "no doubt" Jenkins would be lynched, while the shorter Commercial-Appeal wire said a lynching "will follow the capture of Jenkins."

By December 2 citizens of Tunica County had offered $1,000 for Jenkins "dead or alive," and his father and brother were reported in jail at Tunica. A Columbus Commercial item reprinted in Hattiesburg said the father was believed to have talked with his son after the killing and given him money to get away. The jailed men were later named as Ben and Glen Jenkins, charged with aiding the escape; in February 1904 Ben Jenkins, held as an accessory after the fact, was released on $500 bond with Banks & Co. as sureties.

In early December the city marshal of Cleveland, watching for Jenkins, fired at two Black men who jumped from a train, and a stray bullet killed A. C. Echols, an aged citizen. S. M. Jenkins, a Black resident of Cub Lake, wrote to the Times-Promoter that he was no relation to the accused, and the paper explained that "the high feeling against the murderer" had made him apprehensive. In February 1904 the governor added a $300 reward to $1,000 held on deposit in a Tunica bank, and soon after a Black man named George Jenkins was arrested at Alexandria, Louisiana, where the local sheriff was asked to hold him for Tunica. No report of his return to Mississippi, a trial, or violence against him appears in the coverage.

A short Commercial-Appeal wire ran under "A Mob is in Pursuit of the Negro Slayer" in the Birmingham Age-Herald, "Lynching Slated for Negro" in Morgantown, West Virginia, and "Lynching Expected" in Shiner, Texas. The longer Canton Times version, headed "Murdered by a Negro," called Jenkins "a fiendish negro" of "very bad" reputation, wording the Water Valley Progress repeated. Papers in Hernando and Oxford treated the case as local news, the Times-Promoter headlining it "Foully Murdered" and following the reward, the jailings and the bond. None of these papers questioned the expected lynching, which they reported as a foregone outcome, and no coverage of the case was found in the Black press.

The St. Louis Republic, datelined Memphis, called the second jailed relative George's brother, while the Wausau Pilot called Glen his son, placed the jail at "Tunice, Tenn." and described Clifton as "of Memphis," errors that make it the weaker source.

reader.title: Killing of Herbert Clifton and manhunt for George Jenkins
bases: Armed posses from Tunica and DeSoto counties, one of forty men with bloodhounds, hunted George Jenkins after he was accused of killing Herbert Clifton, and the papers said he would be lynched when caught (A1, A7, A16); no capture or violence against him was reported, so this is a threatened lynching (A21, A26).

Posses of forty and more pursued Jenkins with the stated expectation that he would be 'summarily put to death' for the alleged murder (A7, A1), but no paper reports that he was caught by them or killed; he was still at large in December and a man of that name was arrested by officers in Louisiana in 1904 (A21, A26).
The Commercial-Appeal wire (A1, A7), the local Hernando Times-Promoter (A10, A11) and the Oxford Eagle (A5) independently report the shooting of Clifton, Jenkins's flight and the armed search.

framing.detail: The short wire ran as 'A Mob is in Pursuit of the Negro Slayer', 'Lynching Slated for Negro' and 'Lynching Expected', each stating that 'a lynching will follow the capture'.
The Canton Times and Water Valley Progress called Jenkins 'a fiendish negro' of 'very bad' reputation and reported his summary killing as certain without objection.
The Hernando Times-Promoter headlined 'Foully Murdered' but also printed a Black resident's disclaimer, noting the 'high feeling' that frightened him.
